title: The Rubber Stamp
statementMd:
You have a blank paper strip with $n$ cells, numbered $1$ to $n$ from left to right, and a rubber stamp that prints a fixed word $P$ of length $k$.

Each stamping operation presses the rubber stamp onto the strip, printing the word $P$ across $k$ consecutive cells and overwriting any ink previously there. The stamp may partially hang off either end of the strip; any ink landing outside the strip is lost. Formally, you may place the stamp at any integer position $p$, so that for each $i \in \{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}$, if cell $p + i$ is on the strip ($1 \le p + i \le n$), it receives character $P[i]$.

Given the target string $T$ of length $n$, find the minimum number of stamps needed to make the strip exactly $T$. If it is impossible to obtain the string $T$, print $-1$.

## Input

The first line of the input contains an integer $t$ ($1 \le t \le 10^5$), denoting the number of test cases.

Each test case consists of three lines:

- The first line contains two integers $n$ and $k$ ($1 \le k \le n \le 10^6$), denoting the length of the strip and the length of the stamp word, respectively.
- The second line contains the target string $T$ of length $n$.
- The third line contains the stamp word $P$ of length $k$.

Both strings $T$ and $P$ consist only of lowercase English letters.

It is guaranteed that the sum of $n$ over all test cases does not exceed $10^6$.

## Output

For each test case, print a single integer representing the minimum number of stamps needed to make the strip match $T$, or $-1$ if it is impossible.

## Note

In the first test case of the sample, one optimal sequence of $3$ stamp presses is:

1. Stamp $P = \texttt{"abc"}$ at position $3$ (covering cells $3..5$): the strip becomes `"..abc"`.
2. Stamp $P = \texttt{"abc"}$ at position $5$ (covering cells $5..7$, hanging off the right end so only cell $5$ receives $P[0] = \texttt{'a'}$): the strip becomes `"..aba"`.
3. Stamp $P = \texttt{"abc"}$ at position $1$ (covering cells $1..3$): the strip becomes `"abcba"`.

In the second test case of the sample, one optimal sequence of $3$ stamp presses is:

1. Stamp $P = \texttt{"abc"}$ at position $1$ (covering cells $1..3$): the strip becomes `"abc"`.
2. Stamp $P = \texttt{"abc"}$ at position $-1$ (covering cells $-1..1$, hanging off the left end so cell $1$ receives $P[2] = \texttt{'c'}$): the strip becomes `"cbc"`.
3. Stamp $P = \texttt{"abc"}$ at position $3$ (covering cells $3..5$, hanging off the right end so cell $3$ receives $P[0] = \texttt{'a'}$): the strip becomes `"cba"`.

In the third test case of the sample, any stamp placing `'b'` at cell $i$ simultaneously places `'a'` at cell $i-1$ and `'c'` at cell $i+1$, so no two adjacent cells can both be `'b'`. Thus, it is impossible to produce `"bbbb"`, and the answer is $-1$.
